passages.t: ‘Do not make us cross the Jordan’
passages.happening:
The tribes of Reuben and Gad have ‘very large herds and flocks’. They look at the land east of the Jordan, the lands of Jazer and Gilead, and see that it is good for livestock (verse 1).

They come to Moses, Eleazar and the leaders. “If we have found favor in your sight,” they say, “let this land be given to your servants as a possession. Do not make us cross the Jordan” (verse 5).

Moses answers sharply. “Shall your brothers go to war while you sit here? Why are you discouraging the Israelites from crossing into the land that the LORD has given them?” (verses 6-7). He retells what happened at Kadesh, when the scouts discouraged the people and a generation was lost (verses 8-13). “Now behold, you, a brood of sinners, have risen up in place of your fathers” (verse 14). If they turn away, he says, the whole people may be left in the wilderness again (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Israel now holds the high country east of the Jordan, taken from Sihon and Og. It is upland with good water, well suited to pasture. And for the first time in the book, some of the tribes want to stop before the river.

Their request is not a wicked one. They are herders, and this is herding country. Any people who lived by their flocks would have seen what they saw.

But Moses hears an echo, and it frightens him. Forty years earlier, on another border, ten men said something that took the heart out of everyone else, and a generation died for it. The Hebrew word he uses for ‘discouraging’ in verse 7 is the same word he uses in verse 9 for what the scouts did. If two tribes settle down now, why should the other ten cross a river and fight?

His speech is the story of Numbers in a few sentences: Kadesh, the oath, Caleb and Joshua, the forty years. He is an old man who watched one generation fail at the edge of the land, and he will not watch it happen twice. His words are harsh. He calls them ‘a brood of sinners’ before he has heard them out.

Two things about the request deserve notice. The tribes speak only of their livestock. They do not mention their brothers, or the promise, or God's gift of the land across the river. And they ask to be excused from something the whole people was called to do together. In that world a tribe that left its allies to fight alone was guilty of betrayal. Moses' fear was reasonable, even if their intention turns out to be better than he assumed.
passages.later:
Hebrews sees the same danger in the church, where one person's unbelief can spread to others: “See to it, brothers, that none of you has a wicked heart of unbelief that turns away from the living God” (Hebrews 3:12). Its remedy is that believers should encourage one another every day.

Paul says of the church as one body, “If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).
passages.asks: Reuben and Gad saw good land and thought first of their herds. Ask where a reasonable choice for your own household might take the heart out of others who are depending on you. And ask, with Moses in mind, whether you have ever judged someone's motives before you had heard them through.

passages.t: A promise to cross over armed
passages.happening:
The two tribes come back with an offer. They will build pens for their animals and towns for their families. “But we will arm ourselves and be ready to go ahead of the Israelites until we have brought them into their place” (verse 17). “We will not return to our homes until every Israelite has taken possession of his inheritance” (verse 18).

Moses accepts, on terms. If every armed man crosses the Jordan and stays until the land is subdued, then the eastern land will be theirs (verses 20-22). “But if you do not do this, you will certainly sin against the LORD—and be assured that your sin will find you out” (verse 23).

They agree: “As the LORD has spoken to your servants, so we will do” (verse 31). Moses gives orders about it to Eleazar, to Joshua and to the heads of the tribes (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
The chapter is a negotiation, and it ends better than it began. The earlier generation, rebuked at Kadesh, wept, argued and then marched off to defeat. This generation, rebuked just as sharply, answers with a better plan.

Their offer goes further than Moses asked. They will not only cross with the others. They will go ‘ahead of the Israelites’, in the front. And they will stay until the last tribe has its land. They will leave their families behind and spend years fighting for land that will never be theirs. One phrase is repeated through the chapter: to cross over armed ‘before the LORD’. They bind themselves in God's sight, and not only in Moses'.

Moses makes the agreement formal. It is a conditional contract of a kind common in that world. The terms are stated, the result on each side is spelled out, and it is handed on before witnesses: the priest, the next leader and the heads of families. Moses will be dead before the promise comes due. He makes sure that those who will be alive know about it.

Verse 23 holds a saying that has passed into common speech. The Hebrew verb is ‘to find’. The tribes had asked whether they had ‘found’ favor. Moses warns that a broken promise does not stay hidden. Sin is pictured as something that seeks a person out. In its setting the sentence is about one thing, the breaking of this promise to their brothers. It is a warning against unfaithfulness. It is not a threat held over every anxious conscience.

Moses also quietly corrects their order. They had spoken of pens for their livestock and then towns for their children (verse 16). He answers, ‘Build cities for your little ones and folds for your flocks’ (verse 24). The children come first.
passages.later:
The promise was kept. Joshua reminded the eastern tribes of it before the crossing, and they answered, “Everything you have commanded us we will do, and everywhere you send us we will go” (Joshua 1:16). Years later he sent them home with his thanks (Joshua 22:1-6).

Paul gives the church the same rule in a sentence: “Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).
passages.asks: Two tribes promised to fight for an inheritance they would never share, until every one of their brothers was settled. Ask whose good you are helping to secure that will bring you nothing. And ask what promise you have made to others that you would be tempted to forget once your own needs were met.

passages.happening:
Moses gives the land to Gad, to Reuben and to half the tribe of Manasseh: ‘the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan’ (verse 33).

The Gadites and Reubenites rebuild towns and make folds for their flocks (verses 34-38). Clans of Manasseh take Gilead further north and settle there (verses 39-42).
passages.hearers:
Half of the tribe of Manasseh appears here for the first time in the chapter. With Reuben and Gad it makes up the two and a half tribes that lived east of the river.

Many of the towns named can be placed with fair confidence. Dibon is the modern Dhiban in Jordan. It was there, in 1868, that the Moabite Stone was found, an inscription of Mesha king of Moab from about 840 BC. Mesha boasts of taking Ataroth and Nebo from Israel, and he says that the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old. So an inscription made by one of Israel's enemies agrees that the tribe of Gad was settled in this region. It also shows that the land passed back and forth between Israel and Moab.

Verse 38 notes that some towns were given new names. Several of the old names honored Baal or other gods. Baal-meon is one. The change may mean that the Israelites avoided saying the names of other gods.

The arrangement worked, but the river remained a line through the nation. The book of Joshua tells how an altar built by the eastern tribes beside the Jordan nearly led to war between them and their brothers before it was explained (Joshua 22). And the eastern tribes were the first to be lost. The Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III carried them into exile about 733 to 732 BC, some ten years before the northern capital Samaria fell.

The chapter does not say whether the choice of the east was wise. It records that the request was granted, that the promise was kept, and what came after.
passages.later:
Chronicles records the end of the eastern settlement: God ‘stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria (that is, Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria) to take the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh into exile’ (1 Chronicles 5:26).

The word used in this chapter for a ‘possession’ is the one God used in his promise to Abraham: “And to you and your descendants I will give the land where you are residing—all the land of Canaan—as an eternal possession” (Genesis 17:8).
passages.asks: The eastern tribes chose by what they could see, kept their word, and lived with the results. Ask what choice you are weighing now by what looks good for your own herds. And ask what line that choice might draw between you and the people you belong to.
